gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Mobile Pixels puts the Duex Max DS's draw at 4.5 W, which is exactly the 0.9 A at 5 V a USB 3 Type-A port is guaranteed to supply, so its no-driver fallback (HDMI for video, USB-A for power) runs on a laptop with no video-capable USB-C port; nor that Microsoft requires DisplayPort Alt Mode on every USB-C port of a WHCP-compliant mobile PC under the Windows 11 24H2 requirements.
standout_why: Compared against the three result pages I could open: legitproductreviews.com (cited), deskgearhq.com (cited) and our own dealectric.com/best-laptop-screen-extender-under-300 (cited). All three already say single-cable use needs USB-C with DisplayPort Alt Mode and that mini HDMI is the fallback. legitproductreviews also already says single-screen models avoid the base M1/M2 Mac one-display limit, that brightness is capped on laptop power, and quotes Macworld's 15 W figure for the Float 2 Pro. None gives a wattage for the Duex Max DS, none ties the fallback path to what a USB-A port supplies, and none cites Microsoft's rule; deskgearhq only says the screen draws from the battery 'unless the USB-C port supplies enough wattage', with no number. I could not read deskfinds.com (HTTP 403), itechguides.com, theofficejournal.com or deal.ai, so standout is 2 at most.
decides: It confirms the Duex Max DS as the pick for a shopper who has not named a laptop: one cable on a USB-C port with DisplayPort Alt Mode, and otherwise HDMI plus a USB-A port, which at 4.5 W is powered within the port's guaranteed current with no driver on either path. It also splits our two under-$250 single-screen rows. The Duex Float 2 Pro wants a 15 W source for full brightness (Macworld, as quoted by legitproductreviews), which Microsoft's requirements promise only on USB 40Gbps ports, so the Float suits newer USB4/Thunderbolt laptops or use with a charger. Any laptop with neither a video-capable USB-C port nor HDMI is left out by this mechanism, because the Max DS installation guide shows no USB-A video path.

findings.source_title: How to Choose the Best Portable Monitor for Your MacBook Pro | Mobile Pixels
findings.note: The post says USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode lets video, data and up to 15 W of power share one cable, and that 'Both Duex models include this feature' (the Max DS and the Float).

findings.label: Connection paths, in the maker's order
findings.value: 3 paths: USB-C to C cable alone; USB-C plus HDMI; USB-C cable with USB-A adapter plus HDMI
findings.source_title: Duex Max DS Installation Guide | Mobile Pixels
findings.note: Quotes: 'If your laptop has USB-C port, please directly connect the monitor by using the USB-C to C cable.' 'If your laptop does not work with USB-C to C cable, please also connect the HDMI cable to your laptop.' 'If it does not work with the first two methods, please connect USB- C to C cable with USB-A adapter and HDMI cable.' The page mentions no driver and shows no path that carries video over USB-A, so in the fallback HDMI carries video and USB only powers the screen.

findings.label: Guaranteed current from a USB 3 port (standard downstream port)
findings.note: Quote: 'For USB3, provides guaranteed current of 0.9A @ 5V.' Arithmetic: 0.9 A × 5 V = 4.5 W, equal to Mobile Pixels' 4.5 W figure for the Max DS, so there is no headroom at the guaranteed minimum. The same document gives 0.5 A at 5 V (2.5 W) for USB 2, under the Max DS's draw. This is the ChromiumOS project's document, not the USB-IF specification.

findings.label: Typical current sourced by a USB-C port (ChromeOS devices)
findings.value: 1.5 A at 5 V (7.5 W) typical; up to 3 A at 5 V (15 W) on a single port in certain scenarios
findings.note: Quotes: 'ChromeOS devices currently source power to external USB devices at 5V with a typical current of 1.5A for each Type-C port.' 'In certain scenarios, a single Type-C port can source up to 3A @ 5V.' Watt figures are my arithmetic. Applies to ChromeOS devices as that project describes them.

findings.label: Windows rule on video from USB-C ports
findings.value: DisplayPort Alt Mode required on all USB-C ports of WHCP-compliant mobile PCs (requirements released alongside Windows 11 version 24H2)
findings.source_title: Ending USB-C® Port Confusion (Microsoft USB Blog)
findings.note: By Ugan Sivagnanenthirarajah (Microsoft), published 2025-05-30, updated 2025-09-23. Quotes: 'DisplayPort Alt-Mode is required for all USB-C ports to support connecting monitors.' 'if the PC doesn't support DisplayPort Alternate Mode functionality, that monitor won't light up'. Microsoft adds that 'PC manufacturers are on track to achieve WHCP compliance across most systems in the coming years', so older or non-certified laptops can still have data-only USB-C ports.

findings.label: Minimum power from a USB 40Gbps port on a WHCP-certified PC
findings.value: at least 15 W (7.5 W on tablets)
findings.source_title: Ending USB-C® Port Confusion (Microsoft USB Blog)
findings.note: Quote: 'each USB 40Gbps port sources at least 15 W (7.5 W on tablets).' Also: 'Systems may limit individual port power below 15W' when total requested power exceeds the system's budget. The post's text gives no wattage for 5/10/20 Gbps USB-C ports; its table is an image I could not read.
